name: APACHE II
seoTitle: APACHE II Calculator: Free, With Steps
seoDesc: APACHE II: work out surgery required? from the age and the temperature. A free health calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: surgery required? is what the APACHE II calculator works out, and it gets there from the age, the temperature, the glasgow Coma Scale and the mean arterial pressure. It suits an informed starting point to take to a clinician, not a diagnosis. The panel waits for the button. Edit a field, press Calculate, and compare — one input at a time is enough to see what drives the answer.

sections.title: How does the APACHE II calculator work?
sections.html:
The APACHE II calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports surgery required? in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the history of severe organ insufficiency, the renal failure and the a-a gradient); then you type in the age, the temperature, the glasgow Coma Scale and the mean arterial pressure.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the APACHE II calculator
sections.html:
One relationship drives the whole page:

Surgery required?=glasgow Coma Scale + apache II score − (heart rate) − (respiratory rate) − (age) − (renal failure, creatinine) − (paO₂, a-a gradient, fiO₂) − (hematocrit) − (potassium (K⁺)) − (mean arterial pressure) − (sodium (Na⁺)) − (arterial pH) − (temperature) − (white blood count) − 15

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• The option the calculation settles on.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Temperature, opening in Celsius
  • Pressure, opening in millimeters of mercury
  • Platelet count, opening in platelets per microliter
  • Winters, Na_K, opening in millimoles per liter
  • Winters, Na_K, opening in millimoles per liter
  • Creatinine, opening in milligrams per deciliter

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The APACHE II calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing for an appointment so you can describe your numbers clearly
  • Tracking a measurement over time and understanding what changed
  • Deciding whether a reading is worth a second look
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the age, the temperature and the glasgow Coma Scale — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the APACHE II calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns surgery required?, derived from the age, the temperature and the glasgow Coma Scale. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the APACHE II calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the age, the temperature, the glasgow Coma Scale and the mean arterial pressure, which is 18 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter temperature in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Temperature opens in Celsius and the chip beside it offers 28 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (6 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the APACHE II calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
